A Real Job Queue for Background Work

Why the SLA-breach scan runs on BullMQ and Redis, not a bare setInterval.

The SLA-breach scan is different from every other event in this system: nothing about a request triggers it. It has to notice, on its own, that a ticket has sat open too long — which means something has to run on a schedule, independent of any client ever calling the API. The obvious tool is Node's own setInterval, and it's exactly what this project doesn't use, for reasons that only show up once you ask what happens when things go wrong: what if the scan throws partway through — does it just silently never run again until the process restarts? What if the API process itself restarts — does the timer restart cleanly, or double up? A bare timer has no answer to either question built in.

BullMQ, backed by Redis, is a real job queue: retries with backoff, a schedule that survives a process restart, and a separate worker process actually doing the work, decoupled from the API process that scheduled it.

// Figure 0.4: scheduling a repeatable job (jobs/slaScan.queue.js, excerpt)
export const scheduleSlaScan = async () =>
  slaScanQueue.upsertJobScheduler(
    'sla-scan-repeatable',
    { every: env.SLA_SCAN_INTERVAL_MS },
    {
      name: 'scan',
      opts: {
        attempts: 3,
        backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 5_000 },
      },
    },
  );

attempts: 3 with an exponential backoff is the direct answer to "what if it throws": a failed run gets retried automatically, with a growing delay between attempts, instead of quietly never happening again. upsertJobScheduler with a fixed id is the answer to "what if the process restarts": calling it again replaces the existing schedule rather than stacking up a second one.

Scheduling the job and actually running it are deliberately two separate files: this one only ever queues the work (from the API process), while a second file, run by a completely separate src/worker.js process, is the one that does the scanning. Splitting producer from processor is standard job-queue shape — it's what lets the worker be scaled, restarted, or deployed independently of the API that schedules the work for it.
